title: Medication Guides and REMS at the Pharmacy Counter: 21 CFR Part 208, the Mifepristone REMS and the Removed Clozapine REMS
topic: Federal drug requirements / Medication Guides and risk evaluation and mitigation strategies
subtopic: When and to whom 21 CFR Part 208 requires a Medication Guide, who the authorized dispenser is, what a prescriber's direction under 21 CFR 208.26(b) can and cannot change, FDA's content and format exemptions under 208.26(a) and the supply duties in 208.24; FDA's nonbinding enforcement-discretion guidance for drugs dispensed to a healthcare professional for administration; the elements a REMS may require under 21 U.S.C. 355-1(e) and (f); the current Mifepristone REMS Program's prescriber and pharmacy certification requirements; and what FDA's removal of the Clozapine REMS changed for pharmacies and what the clozapine labeling still carries
learning_objectives: State when 21 CFR Part 208 requires a Medication Guide to be provided, including its application to refill prescriptions, and identify the authorized dispenser on whom 21 CFR 208.24(e) places the duty.
Apply 21 CFR 208.24(e) to a product collected by the patient's agent and explain why the Guide is provided at the time of dispensing.
State what a prescriber's direction under 21 CFR 208.26(b) can do, and what a patient's request for information does to that direction.
Distinguish FDA's power under 21 CFR 208.26(a) to exempt or defer content and format requirements from any discretion at the counter, and name the two requirements FDA may not exempt.
Separate the manufacturer's and the distributor's or packer's duties in 21 CFR 208.24(a)-(c) from the authorized dispenser's duty, and state the effect of 21 CFR 208.24(f).

Explain FDA's nonbinding enforcement-discretion policy for drugs dispensed to a healthcare professional for administration, and identify when the policy still expects a Guide, including on a request by the patient or the patient's agent.
List the elements 21 U.S.C. 355-1 allows a REMS to include and identify which of them can reach a dispensing pharmacy.

Apply the current Mifepristone REMS Program at a pharmacy: certification, prescriber verification, the 4-calendar-day delivery standard and its prescriber-confirmation route, NDC and lot recording, and the limits on transfers.
Allocate the Mifepristone REMS requirements correctly among the certified prescriber, the certified pharmacy, the patient and the Mifepristone Sponsors.
State what FDA's removal of the Clozapine REMS ended for pharmacies and what the clozapine labeling still carries, including a Medication Guide.

orientation.text: A Medication Guide is FDA-approved patient labeling, and 21 CFR Part 208 decides when one has to be handed over at the counter. Under 21 CFR 208.1(a) the part reaches human prescription drug products, including biological products, that FDA determines pose a serious and significant public health concern requiring distribution of FDA-approved patient information. It applies primarily to products used on an outpatient basis without direct supervision by a health professional, and it states in terms that it applies to new prescriptions and refill prescriptions, so the Guide is not a first-fill document. Not every prescription drug has one. Under 21 CFR 208.1(c) patient labeling will be required if FDA determines that one or more of three circumstances exists: patient labeling could help prevent serious adverse effects; the product has serious risks, relative to benefits, of which patients should be made aware because the information could affect their decision to use, or to continue to use, the product; or the product is important to health and patient adherence to directions for use is crucial to its effectiveness. The determination is FDA's, and 21 CFR 208.1(b) describes the purpose as providing information when FDA determines in writing that it is necessary to patients' safe and effective use. The pharmacy sees the result on the product itself: under 21 CFR 208.24(d) the label of each container, or of the package where the container label is too small, instructs the authorized dispenser to provide a Medication Guide to each patient to whom the product is dispensed and states how the Guide is provided.

The dispensing duty sits in 21 CFR 208.24(e). Each authorized dispenser of a prescription drug product for which a Medication Guide is required shall, when the product is dispensed to a patient or to a patient's agent, provide a Medication Guide directly to each patient or to the patient's agent, unless an exemption applies under 21 CFR 208.26. Three definitions in 21 CFR 208.3 control how that sentence works. An authorized dispenser is an individual licensed, registered, or otherwise permitted by the jurisdiction in which the individual practices to provide drug products on prescription in the course of professional practice, so the duty is framed around an individual such as the dispensing pharmacist rather than around the pharmacy as a business. To dispense to patients includes delivery by an authorized dispenser or by an agent of an authorized dispenser under a lawful prescription, so a product handed over at the register by another member of staff has still been dispensed and the dispenser's duty has attached. And a patient is any individual with respect to whom a drug product is intended to be, or has been, used, while the product may be dispensed either to that patient or to the patient's agent; Part 208 does not define the agent or distinguish among the people who collect on a patient's behalf. The Guide therefore goes to whichever of them receives the product, at the time it is dispensed. Holding the Guide back for the patient's next visit, or leaving copies where patients may pick them up, does not provide it directly to the patient or the agent.

21 CFR 208.26(b) gives the prescriber one narrow power and qualifies it in the next sentence. If the licensed practitioner who prescribes a product subject to Part 208 determines that it is not in a particular patient's best interest to receive a Medication Guide because of significant concerns about the effect of a Medication Guide, the practitioner may direct that the Guide not be provided to that particular patient. The direction is the prescriber's, it rests on a determination about one patient, and nothing in the paragraph lets a pharmacist make the same determination. However, the authorized dispenser shall provide a Medication Guide to any patient who requests information when the drug product is dispensed, regardless of any such direction by the licensed practitioner. Two features of that sentence decide most questions. The trigger is a request for information made when the product is dispensed; the text does not require the request to be written or to name the Medication Guide. And the paragraph resolves the conflict itself, so honouring the request does not wait on the prescriber's agreement. Where the patient requests nothing, the direction operates as an exemption under 21 CFR 208.26 for that patient, and 21 CFR 208.24(e) does not then require the Guide to be provided to that patient.

The other exemption in 21 CFR 208.26 is not exercised at the counter at all. Under 21 CFR 208.26(a) FDA, on its own initiative or in response to a written request from an applicant, may exempt or defer any Medication Guide content or format requirement on the basis that the requirement is inapplicable, unnecessary, or contrary to patients' best interests. Two requirements are beyond that power: 21 CFR 208.20(a)(2), under which the Guide must be scientifically accurate and based on, and not in conflict with, the approved professional labeling, and 21 CFR 208.20(a)(6), under which the words Medication Guide appear prominently at the top of the first page and FDA's verbatim approval statement appears at the bottom. The power belongs to FDA and concerns what the Guide says and how it is presented, so it gives a pharmacist no basis for deciding that a Guide is unnecessary. The rest of 21 CFR 208.24 explains how the Guide reaches the counter. The manufacturer obtains FDA approval of the Guide before it may be distributed, and each manufacturer who ships a container of the product is responsible for ensuring that Guides are available, by providing either Guides or the means to produce them in sufficient numbers to distributors, packers or authorized dispensers to permit the authorized dispenser to provide a Guide to each patient receiving a prescription for the product. A distributor or packer that receives Guides, or the means to produce them, provides them to each authorized dispenser to whom it ships a container of the product. Finally, 21 CFR 208.24(f) provides that an authorized dispenser or wholesaler is not subject to section 510 of the Federal Food, Drug, and Cosmetic Act, the registration and listing requirement for producers of drugs, solely because of an act it performs under Part 208.

Part 208 is written with outpatient use in mind, and FDA's position on a drug dispensed to a health care professional who then administers it is set out in guidance rather than in the regulation. FDA's final guidance Medication Guides — Distribution Requirements and Inclusion in Risk Evaluation and Mitigation Strategies (REMS), issued in November 2011, contains nonbinding recommendations and describes when FDA intends to exercise enforcement discretion. In that sense a Medication Guide need not be provided when a drug is dispensed to a healthcare professional for administration to a patient in an inpatient setting, or in an outpatient setting such as a clinic or dialysis or infusion center, except in the circumstances the guidance lists. The exceptions carry most of the weight. A Guide must be provided when the patient or the patient's agent requests one, in every setting. It must be provided the first time a drug is dispensed to a healthcare professional for administration to a patient in an outpatient setting, and the first time a drug is dispensed in an outpatient setting of any kind after the Guide is materially changed. Where a drug's REMS includes specific requirements for reviewing or providing a Guide as part of an element to assure safe use, the Guide is provided in accordance with the REMS. And where a drug is dispensed in an outpatient setting such as a retail pharmacy or a hospital ambulatory care pharmacy and will then be used by the patient without direct supervision by a healthcare professional, the enforcement discretion does not apply; the guidance's table expects a Guide each time a drug is dispensed directly to a patient or caregiver. The policy describes how FDA intends to enforce Part 208; it is not one of the exemptions in 21 CFR 208.26.

A risk evaluation and mitigation strategy is a different instrument with a different source. Under 21 U.S.C. 355-1(a)(1), when FDA determines that a REMS is necessary to ensure that the benefits of a drug outweigh its risks and informs the person submitting the application, that person submits a proposed REMS as part of the application, so each REMS is built for a particular drug. The statute supplies the menu. Under 21 U.S.C. 355-1(e) a REMS may require that the responsible person develop, for distribution to each patient when the drug is dispensed, a Medication Guide as provided for under 21 CFR Part 208 and, where FDA determines it may help mitigate a serious risk, a patient package insert; that the responsible person conduct a communication plan to health care providers; and, for a drug with a serious risk of an adverse drug experience from overdose or abuse, that the drug be made available for dispensing to certain patients in unit dose packaging, packaging that provides a set duration or another packaging system, or be dispensed to certain patients with safe disposal packaging or a safe disposal system. Under 21 U.S.C. 355-1(f)(3) elements to assure safe use may require that prescribers have particular training or experience or be specially certified; that pharmacies, practitioners, or health care settings that dispense the drug be specially certified; that the drug be dispensed to patients only in certain health care settings, such as hospitals; that it be dispensed with evidence or other documentation of safe-use conditions, such as laboratory test results; that each patient be subject to certain monitoring; or that each patient be enrolled in a registry. Under 21 U.S.C. 355-1(f)(4) some of those elements may include a system through which the applicant is able to take reasonable steps to monitor, evaluate and work to improve implementation by health care providers, pharmacists and others. None of these elements is one that every REMS must contain; each is an element FDA may require for a particular drug on the determination the statute describes. What a REMS asks of a dispensing pharmacy therefore depends on the elements FDA has required for that drug, which is why the requirements are read from that product's current REMS rather than borrowed from another.

The Mifepristone REMS Program is the single shared system REMS for mifepristone 200 mg, which FDA describes as setting the requirements that must be followed for prescribing and dispensing mifepristone for medical termination of pregnancy through ten weeks gestation, and its current REMS document records a most recent modification in September 2025. The program's present shape dates from a modification FDA approved on January 3, 2023, which removed the former in-person dispensing requirement and added pharmacy certification; FDA states that under the program mifepristone may be dispensed in person or by mail, and that the program does not require a patient to see a health care provider in person before obtaining mifepristone. Its first element to assure safe use is that healthcare providers who prescribe mifepristone must be specially certified. To become certified a provider reviews the Prescribing Information and completes a Prescriber Agreement Form, agreeing to having the ability to assess the duration of pregnancy accurately, the ability to diagnose ectopic pregnancies, and the ability to provide surgical intervention in cases of incomplete abortion or severe bleeding or to have made plans to provide such care through others, together with the ability to assure patient access to medical facilities equipped to provide blood transfusions and resuscitation, if necessary. As a condition of certification the prescriber must ensure that the Patient Agreement Form is reviewed with the patient and the risks of the treatment regimen fully explained, that the patient's questions are answered before the patient receives mifepristone, that the provider and the patient sign the form, that the patient is given a copy of the form and of the Medication Guide, and that the signed form is placed in the patient's medical record. The REMS certifies healthcare providers who prescribe; FDA notes that some states allow providers other than physicians to prescribe medications and that providers should check their individual state laws.

Dispensing is where the pharmacy enters, and the REMS states the pharmacy's part in detail. Mifepristone may be dispensed only by or under the supervision of a certified prescriber, or by a certified pharmacy on a prescription issued by a certified prescriber. A pharmacy becomes certified by being able to receive Prescriber Agreement Forms by email and fax, being able to ship mifepristone using a shipping service that provides tracking information, designating an authorized representative to carry out the certification process on its behalf, and ensuring that the representative oversees implementation and compliance, which includes reviewing the Prescribing Information and completing a Pharmacy Agreement Form. By signing, the representative agrees that the pharmacy will put processes and procedures in place to verify that the prescriber is certified, by confirming that the completed Prescriber Agreement Form was received with the prescription or is on file; to dispense so that the drug is delivered to the patient within 4 calendar days of the date the pharmacy receives the prescription, or, for a patient who will receive it later than that, to confirm the appropriateness of dispensing with the prescriber and document the prescriber's decision; to record the NDC and lot number from each package dispensed in the patient's record; to track and verify receipt of each shipment; to dispense the drug in its package as supplied by the Mifepristone Sponsor; to report any patient death to the prescriber with the NDC and lot number, remind the prescriber of the obligation to report it to the Sponsor, and notify the Sponsor that the pharmacy has reported to the prescriber; not to distribute, transfer, loan or sell mifepristone except to certified prescribers or other locations of the pharmacy; to keep records of Prescriber Agreement Forms, of dispensing and shipping, and of its processes and procedures and compliance with them; to keep the identity of the patient and prescriber confidential, limiting access to the personnel necessary to dispense under the program or as necessary for payment and/or insurance purposes; to train all relevant staff; and to comply with audits carried out by the Mifepristone Sponsors or a third party acting on their behalf. FDA states that the January 2023 modification removed the restriction that did not allow retail pharmacies to dispense mifepristone and that any pharmacy that meets the program requirements is eligible for certification.

Keeping the actors apart answers most mifepristone questions. The Patient Agreement Form belongs to the certified prescriber and the patient: the patient signs it to indicate having received, read and been provided a copy of it and having received counseling from the healthcare provider regarding the risk of serious complications, and the REMS requires mifepristone to be dispensed with evidence or other documentation of safe use conditions as ensured by the certified prescriber in signing the Prescriber Agreement Form. When a certified pharmacy will dispense, the prescriber provides that pharmacy with a signed Prescriber Agreement Form and assesses the appropriateness of dispensing when the pharmacy makes contact about a patient who will receive the drug more than 4 calendar days after the pharmacy received the prescription. A certified prescriber who dispenses mifepristone or supervises its dispensing provides an authorized distributor with a signed Prescriber Agreement Form and ensures that the NDC and lot number from each package dispensed are recorded in the patient's record. The Mifepristone Sponsors must de-certify pharmacies that do not maintain compliance, verify annually that the name and contact information of a certified pharmacy's authorized representative are current and, if they differ, require the pharmacy to recertify with the new authorized representative, and audit a certified pharmacy within 180 calendar days after it places its first order and annually thereafter if it has ordered in the previous 12 months, while distributors ship mifepristone only to certified pharmacies or locations identified by certified prescribers. The REMS also makes the certified prescriber responsible for ensuring that the patient is provided with the Medication Guide. Nothing in the REMS document displaces 21 CFR 208.24(e), so the pharmacist who dispenses mifepristone for a certified pharmacy remains an authorized dispenser with that regulation's duty to provide the Guide when the product is dispensed.

Clozapine shows a REMS being taken away while the patient labeling stays. FDA removed the Clozapine REMS effective June 13, 2025. The removed REMS had required enrollment of prescribers, pharmacies and patients in a restricted distribution program and reporting of the absolute neutrophil count (ANC), and FDA states that prescribers, pharmacies and patients are no longer required to participate in the REMS program and report patients' ANC results to the REMS in order for clozapine to be dispensed. For pharmacies FDA spells out two consequences: pharmacies do not need to be enrolled in the REMS to order clozapine from wholesaler distributors, and pharmacists do not need to verify patient eligibility, including ANC monitoring, before dispensing clozapine to patients. What did not change is the risk. FDA states that severe neutropenia remains a serious, potentially fatal risk, that information about it is in the prescribing information for all clozapine medicines, including in a Boxed Warning and a new Medication Guide, and that FDA recommends that prescribers monitor patients' ANC according to the monitoring frequencies described in the prescribing information and counsel patients about the risk of severe neutropenia. That recommendation is addressed to prescribers and is not stated as a condition of dispensing. The Medication Guide, by contrast, is FDA-approved patient labeling within the definition in 21 CFR 208.3, so the duty in 21 CFR 208.24(e) reaches clozapine as it reaches any product for which a Guide is required. FDA's 2011 guidance anticipates the arrangement: all Medication Guides must meet the standard and requirements in Part 208, not every newly required Guide is an element of a REMS, and FDA may approve a Guide under Part 208 without requiring a REMS.

Everything taught here is federal. Part 208 and 21 U.S.C. 355-1 are federal law, the enforcement discretion policy is nonbinding FDA guidance, and the Mifepristone REMS requirements are set by the approved REMS document for that product. Part 208 and the REMS requirements taught here apply to a pharmacist and pharmacy in Massachusetts alongside Massachusetts law, and where both reach the same dispensing the pharmacist satisfies both, so the stricter requirement governs. Three Massachusetts subjects sit next to this one and are taught in their own sections. Counseling is the first: Part 208 regulates the provision of a document and says nothing about an offer to counsel, and 21 CFR 208.24(e) yields only to an exemption under 21 CFR 208.26, which a patient's declining to discuss the medication is not. The container label and the dispensing record are the second. Prospective drug review is the third, and FDA's removal of the clozapine eligibility check says nothing about it. Controlled-substance rules generally are also outside this section.

worked_examples.scenario: A pharmacist dispenses the third refill of a product whose container label instructs the dispenser to provide a Medication Guide. The patient's adult son collects it. A technician suggests leaving the Guide out, because the patient received one with the first fill and the son is not the patient.
steps: Start with the reach of the regulation. 21 CFR 208.1(a) applies Part 208 to new prescriptions and refill prescriptions, so a refill does not take the product outside it.

Confirm that a Guide is required for this product. Under 21 CFR 208.24(d) the container label, or the package label where the container label is too small, instructs the authorized dispenser to provide a Medication Guide to each patient to whom the product is dispensed.

Identify the recipient. 21 CFR 208.24(e) requires the authorized dispenser, when the product is dispensed to a patient or to a patient's agent, to provide a Medication Guide directly to the patient or to the patient's agent; the son collecting for his parent is the person to whom the product is being dispensed.

Look for an exemption under 21 CFR 208.26. There is no prescriber direction to consider, and an FDA exemption or deferral under 21 CFR 208.26(a) would concern the Guide's content or format, not whether it is handed over.

Check FDA's enforcement policy for completeness. Its November 2011 guidance expects a Guide each time a drug is dispensed directly to a patient or caregiver in an outpatient setting such as a retail pharmacy.
worked_examples.resolution: The Guide goes to the son with the refill. The error the scenario invites is treating the Medication Guide as a first-fill document, and treating anyone other than the patient as unable to receive it.

worked_examples.scenario: A prescriber tells the pharmacy that, for one particular patient, she has determined that a Medication Guide is not in the patient's best interest because of significant concerns about its effect, and directs that it not be provided. When the patient collects the prescription he asks the pharmacist whether there is anything he can read about the medicine. A colleague suggests calling the prescriber before giving him anything.
steps: Read what the prescriber may do. Under 21 CFR 208.26(b) the licensed practitioner who prescribes the product and determines that a Guide is not in a particular patient's best interest because of significant concerns about its effect may direct that it not be provided to that patient.

Read the next sentence before acting on the direction. The authorized dispenser shall provide a Medication Guide to any patient who requests information when the drug product is dispensed, regardless of any such direction by the licensed practitioner.

Test the facts against that trigger. The patient asked for something to read about the medicine when it was dispensed; the text requires a request for information, not a written request and not a request that names the Medication Guide.
Reject the call to the prescriber as a precondition. The paragraph resolves the conflict itself, so the Guide is provided without first obtaining the prescriber's agreement.

Note what the direction would have done without the request. Had the patient asked for nothing, the direction would have operated as an exemption under 21 CFR 208.26 for him, and 21 CFR 208.24(e) would not have required the Guide.
worked_examples.resolution: The pharmacist provides the Medication Guide now. The error the scenario invites is treating the prescriber's lawful direction as final, or routing the patient's request back to the prescriber for permission.

worked_examples.scenario: A hospital pharmacy prepares a drug whose labeling includes a Medication Guide. Some doses go to the hospital's outpatient infusion center, where nurses administer the drug to a patient every week; others go to inpatients on the wards. A newly hired pharmacist believes Part 208 requires a Guide with every dose in both places. At the fourth weekly infusion the patient asks for the Guide.
steps: Start with the regulation. 21 CFR 208.1(a) says Part 208 applies primarily to products used on an outpatient basis without direct supervision by a health professional, and 21 CFR 208.24(e) attaches the duty when a product is dispensed to a patient or to a patient's agent.

Turn to FDA's policy for administration settings. FDA's November 2011 guidance, which contains nonbinding recommendations, states that FDA intends to exercise enforcement discretion, so that a Guide need not be provided, when a drug is dispensed to a healthcare professional for administration to a patient in an inpatient setting or in an outpatient setting such as an infusion center, except in the circumstances it lists.

Apply the listed circumstances to the infusion center. A Guide is expected the first time the drug is dispensed to a healthcare professional for administration there, and the first time it is dispensed after the Guide is materially changed, but not with every later dose.
Apply them to the wards. For inpatients the guidance's table shows enforcement discretion for each dispensing, for the first dispensing and after a material change.

Apply the request. The guidance states that a Guide must be provided when the patient or the patient's agent requests one, in every setting, so the request at the fourth infusion is answered with the Guide.
Check for a REMS. If the drug's REMS included specific requirements for reviewing or providing the Guide as part of an element to assure safe use, the Guide would be provided as the REMS specifies.
worked_examples.resolution: Neither location needs a Guide with every dose, but the infusion center needed one at the first dispensing and must answer the patient's request. The error the scenario invites is reading FDA's enforcement discretion either as a blanket exemption for administered drugs or as a rule written into Part 208, when it is nonbinding enforcement policy with exceptions.

worked_examples.scenario: A community pharmacy in Massachusetts that is certified in the Mifepristone REMS Program receives an electronic prescription for mifepristone 200 mg. No Prescriber Agreement Form came with the prescription and none is on file. The patient will not be able to take delivery for six days. To avoid waiting for its own order, a staff member proposes borrowing a package from a nearby certified pharmacy owned by a different company.
steps: Confirm the pharmacy may dispense at all. Mifepristone may be dispensed only by or under the supervision of a certified prescriber, or by a certified pharmacy on a prescription issued by a certified prescriber, and a retail pharmacy that meets the program requirements is eligible for certification.

Verify the prescriber first. The pharmacy has agreed to verify that the prescriber is certified by confirming that the completed Prescriber Agreement Form was received with the prescription or is on file; neither is true here, so the prescription cannot yet be treated as issued by a certified prescriber. Under the REMS it is the certified prescriber who provides a certified pharmacy with a signed Prescriber Agreement Form.

Apply the delivery period. The pharmacy dispenses so that the drug is delivered to the patient within 4 calendar days of the date it receives the prescription; because this patient will receive it more than 4 calendar days after that date, the pharmacy confirms the appropriateness of dispensing with the prescriber and documents the prescriber's decision.

Refuse the loan. Each certified pharmacy agrees not to distribute, transfer, loan or sell mifepristone except to certified prescribers or other locations of the pharmacy, so a pharmacy owned by a different company cannot lend its stock consistently with its own agreement, and distributors ship mifepristone only to certified pharmacies or locations identified by certified prescribers.

Complete the dispensing correctly. The pharmacy records the NDC and lot number from the package in the patient's record, dispenses the drug in its package as supplied by the Mifepristone Sponsor, and the dispensing pharmacist provides the Medication Guide under 21 CFR 208.24(e).
worked_examples.resolution: The pharmacy must first obtain confirmation of the prescriber's certification through a Prescriber Agreement Form, then confirm with the prescriber and document whether dispensing for delivery after 4 calendar days is appropriate, and it may not borrow stock from another company's pharmacy. The error the scenario invites is treating certification as the pharmacy's only obligation, and treating the 4-calendar-day period as either irrelevant or an absolute bar.

worked_examples.scenario: In September 2026 a patient brings a new clozapine prescription to a pharmacy. A pharmacist who trained years earlier says the pharmacy must first confirm the patient's REMS enrollment and a current ANC through the REMS, and adds that with no REMS there is no Medication Guide to give. The pharmacy's buyer separately asks whether the wholesaler will require REMS enrollment before shipping.
steps: Date the program. FDA removed the Clozapine REMS effective June 13, 2025, so there is no REMS to consult on these facts.

State what ended for the pharmacy. FDA states that pharmacies do not need to be enrolled in the REMS to order clozapine from wholesaler distributors and that pharmacists do not need to verify patient eligibility, including ANC monitoring, before dispensing clozapine.

State what did not end. FDA states that severe neutropenia remains a serious, potentially fatal risk, that the prescribing information for all clozapine medicines carries it in a Boxed Warning and a new Medication Guide, and that FDA recommends that prescribers monitor ANC according to the prescribing information.

Apply Part 208 to the Guide. A Medication Guide is FDA-approved patient labeling within the definition in 21 CFR 208.3, so under 21 CFR 208.24(e) the dispensing pharmacist provides it when clozapine is dispensed to the patient or the patient's agent.
Keep the monitoring recommendation with its addressee. FDA directs the ANC-monitoring recommendation to prescribers and does not state it as a condition of dispensing.
worked_examples.resolution: No REMS enrollment or REMS verification of ANC is a condition of ordering or dispensing, but the Medication Guide is provided with the prescription. The error the scenario invites is tying the Guide to the REMS, so that the removal of one is taken to remove the other, alongside the stale belief that the enrollment gate survives.

retrieval_prompts.prompt: Does 21 CFR Part 208 apply to refill prescriptions?
retrieval_prompts.answer: Yes. 21 CFR 208.1(a) states that Part 208 applies to new prescriptions and refill prescriptions.

retrieval_prompts.prompt: Who is an authorized dispenser under 21 CFR 208.3(a)?
retrieval_prompts.answer: An individual licensed, registered, or otherwise permitted by the jurisdiction in which the individual practices to provide drug products on prescription in the course of professional practice.

retrieval_prompts.prompt: Name the three circumstances in 21 CFR 208.1(c), any one of which leads FDA to require patient labeling.
retrieval_prompts.answer: Patient labeling could help prevent serious adverse effects; the product has serious risks, relative to benefits, of which patients should be made aware because the information could affect the decision to use or continue to use it; or the product is important to health and adherence to directions for use is crucial to its effectiveness.

retrieval_prompts.prompt: To whom, and when, does 21 CFR 208.24(e) require the authorized dispenser to provide the Medication Guide?
retrieval_prompts.answer: Directly to each patient or to the patient's agent, when the product is dispensed to the patient or to the patient's agent, unless an exemption applies under 21 CFR 208.26.

retrieval_prompts.prompt: What may a prescriber direct under 21 CFR 208.26(b), and on what basis?
retrieval_prompts.answer: That the Medication Guide not be provided to a particular patient, where the prescriber determines that receiving it is not in that patient's best interest because of significant concerns about the effect of a Medication Guide.

retrieval_prompts.prompt: A prescriber has directed that a patient not receive the Guide, and the patient asks for information at pickup. What does the authorized dispenser do?
retrieval_prompts.answer: Provides the Medication Guide. 21 CFR 208.26(b) requires the authorized dispenser to provide it to any patient who requests information when the product is dispensed, regardless of the prescriber's direction.

retrieval_prompts.prompt: Under 21 CFR 208.26(a), who may exempt or defer a Medication Guide requirement, and which requirements are beyond that power?
retrieval_prompts.answer: FDA, on its own initiative or on an applicant's written request, may exempt or defer content or format requirements, but not 21 CFR 208.20(a)(2) (scientific accuracy and consistency with approved labeling) or 208.20(a)(6) (the Medication Guide title and the FDA-approval statement).

retrieval_prompts.prompt: Who must obtain FDA approval of a Medication Guide, and what does a distributor or packer do with the Guides it receives?
retrieval_prompts.answer: The manufacturer, before the Guide may be distributed, under 21 CFR 208.24(a). A distributor or packer provides the Guides, or the means to produce them, to each authorized dispenser to whom it ships a container of the product, under 21 CFR 208.24(c).

retrieval_prompts.prompt: Does acting under Part 208, such as producing Medication Guides from means supplied by the manufacturer, make an authorized dispenser subject to section 510 registration?
retrieval_prompts.answer: Not by itself. Under 21 CFR 208.24(f) an authorized dispenser or wholesaler is not subject to section 510 solely because of an act performed under Part 208.

retrieval_prompts.prompt: Under FDA's November 2011 guidance, when must a Medication Guide still be provided for a drug dispensed to a healthcare professional for administration in an outpatient setting?
retrieval_prompts.answer: When the patient or the patient's agent requests one; the first time the drug is dispensed to a healthcare professional for administration there; the first time it is dispensed in an outpatient setting after the Guide is materially changed; and as a REMS specifies where it includes specific requirements for reviewing or providing the Guide as part of an element to assure safe use.

retrieval_prompts.prompt: Is FDA's enforcement discretion for drugs administered to inpatients an exemption written into 21 CFR Part 208?
retrieval_prompts.answer: No. It is a statement in nonbinding FDA guidance of when FDA intends to exercise enforcement discretion; the exemptions in the regulation are those in 21 CFR 208.26.

retrieval_prompts.prompt: List the six requirements that elements to assure safe use may impose under 21 U.S.C. 355-1(f)(3).
retrieval_prompts.answer: Prescriber training, experience or special certification; special certification of pharmacies, practitioners, or health care settings that dispense; dispensing only in certain health care settings; dispensing with evidence or other documentation of safe-use conditions; patient monitoring; and patient enrollment in a registry.

retrieval_prompts.prompt: Does every REMS require the dispensing pharmacy to be certified?
retrieval_prompts.answer: No. Special certification of dispensers is one element 21 U.S.C. 355-1(f)(3)(B) permits FDA to require in a REMS; whether a pharmacy must be certified depends on the elements FDA has required in the REMS for the particular drug.

retrieval_prompts.prompt: Under the current Mifepristone REMS Program, who may dispense mifepristone?
retrieval_prompts.answer: A certified prescriber or someone under a certified prescriber's supervision, or a certified pharmacy on a prescription issued by a certified prescriber.

retrieval_prompts.prompt: Name the four steps or capabilities a pharmacy needs to become certified in the Mifepristone REMS Program.
retrieval_prompts.answer: Ability to receive Prescriber Agreement Forms by email and fax; ability to ship using a shipping service that provides tracking information; designation of an authorized representative to carry out certification; and oversight of implementation and compliance by that representative, including reviewing the Prescribing Information and completing a Pharmacy Agreement Form.

retrieval_prompts.prompt: A certified pharmacy's patient will not receive mifepristone until 6 calendar days after the pharmacy received the prescription. What does the REMS require?
retrieval_prompts.answer: The pharmacy confirms the appropriateness of dispensing with the prescriber and documents the prescriber's decision, because the standard is delivery within 4 calendar days of the date the pharmacy receives the prescription.

retrieval_prompts.prompt: Under the Mifepristone REMS, who ensures that the patient receives a copy of the Patient Agreement Form and the Medication Guide?
retrieval_prompts.answer: The certified prescriber, as a condition of certification.

retrieval_prompts.prompt: Does the current Mifepristone REMS Program require in-person dispensing?
retrieval_prompts.answer: No. FDA states that the January 2023 modification removed the in-person dispensing requirement and that under the program mifepristone may be dispensed in person or by mail.

retrieval_prompts.prompt: To whom may a certified pharmacy distribute, transfer, loan or sell mifepristone?
retrieval_prompts.answer: Only to certified prescribers or other locations of the pharmacy.

retrieval_prompts.prompt: Since June 13, 2025, what REMS step does a pharmacy need before ordering or dispensing clozapine?
retrieval_prompts.answer: None. FDA removed the Clozapine REMS; pharmacies do not need to be enrolled to order from wholesaler distributors, and pharmacists do not need to verify patient eligibility, including ANC monitoring, before dispensing.

retrieval_prompts.prompt: What does clozapine labeling carry about severe neutropenia after the REMS removal, and what follows at the counter?
retrieval_prompts.answer: A Boxed Warning and a new Medication Guide in the prescribing information; the Medication Guide is provided by the authorized dispenser under 21 CFR 208.24(e) when clozapine is dispensed.

quick_review.text: Part 208 applies to new prescriptions and refill prescriptions, primarily for products used on an outpatient basis without direct supervision by a health professional.
A Medication Guide is required when FDA determines that one of the three circumstances in 21 CFR 208.1(c) exists; not every prescription drug has one.
The authorized dispenser is an individual permitted by the jurisdiction to provide drug products on prescription in professional practice, and delivery by the dispenser's agent is still dispensing.

When a product that requires a Guide is dispensed to the patient or the patient's agent, the authorized dispenser provides the Guide directly to that person unless an exemption under 21 CFR 208.26 applies.
The container label, or the package label where the container label is too small, instructs the dispenser to provide a Guide and states how it is provided.

A prescriber may direct that a particular patient not receive the Guide because of significant concerns about its effect, but a patient who requests information when the product is dispensed receives it regardless.
FDA may exempt or defer Guide content or format requirements on its own initiative or an applicant's written request, but not the requirements in 21 CFR 208.20(a)(2) and (a)(6).

The manufacturer obtains FDA approval of the Guide and ensures Guides or the means to produce them are available; distributors and packers pass them on; acting under Part 208 does not by itself subject a dispenser to section 510.

FDA's nonbinding 2011 guidance describes enforcement discretion for drugs dispensed to healthcare professionals for administration, but a Guide is still expected on request, at the first outpatient administration dispensing, at the first outpatient dispensing after a material change, and as a REMS specifies.
A REMS is product-specific; 21 U.S.C. 355-1 lets FDA require a Medication Guide, a patient package insert, a communication plan, packaging or disposal measures, and elements to assure safe use.

Pharmacy certification, dispensing only in certain health care settings and dispensing only with documentation of safe-use conditions are elements a particular REMS may require, not duties that every REMS imposes.

Mifepristone is prescribed by a certified prescriber and dispensed by or under the supervision of a certified prescriber, or by a certified pharmacy on a certified prescriber's prescription; retail pharmacies are eligible for certification.

A certified pharmacy verifies the prescriber's Prescriber Agreement Form, dispenses for delivery within 4 calendar days of receiving the prescription or confirms appropriateness with the prescriber and documents the decision, records NDC and lot numbers, and transfers stock only to certified prescribers or its own other locations.
The certified prescriber, not the pharmacy, handles the Patient Agreement Form and ensures the patient receives a copy of it and of the Medication Guide.

The Clozapine REMS was removed effective June 13, 2025: no enrollment to order and no eligibility or ANC verification before dispensing, while the Boxed Warning, a new Medication Guide and FDA's recommendation that prescribers monitor ANC remain.

decision_logic.condition: A product is presented for dispensing, new or refill.
decision_logic.action: Check the container label, or the package label where the container label is too small, for the instruction to provide a Medication Guide; if it is there, Part 208 governs this dispensing whether the prescription is new or a refill.

decision_logic.condition: Someone other than the patient is collecting the product.
decision_logic.action: Provide the Guide directly to the person collecting as the patient's agent at the time of dispensing, rather than holding it for the patient.

decision_logic.condition: The prescriber has directed that this patient not receive the Guide.
decision_logic.action: Ask whether the patient has requested information at the time of dispensing. If so, provide the Guide regardless of the direction; if not, the direction operates as an exemption for that patient.

decision_logic.condition: Someone suggests the Guide is unnecessary for a patient or a product.
decision_logic.action: Look for a basis in 21 CFR 208.26: a prescriber's direction for a particular patient under 208.26(b), which yields to the patient's request, or an FDA exemption or deferral under 208.26(a), which concerns content or format and is granted by FDA rather than at the counter. A patient's declining to discuss the medication is neither.

decision_logic.condition: The drug is dispensed to a healthcare professional for administration to a patient.
decision_logic.action: Apply FDA's nonbinding enforcement policy. In an inpatient setting a Guide need not be provided unless the patient or the patient's agent requests one or a REMS so provides; in an outpatient administration setting provide it the first time the drug is dispensed there, the first time after a material change, on request, and as a REMS specifies.

decision_logic.condition: The product is subject to a REMS.
decision_logic.action: Read the current approved REMS for that product and identify which of its elements reach dispensers, such as pharmacy certification, dispensing only in certain health care settings or dispensing with documentation of safe-use conditions; do not import requirements from another product's REMS.

decision_logic.condition: A mifepristone prescription arrives at a pharmacy.
decision_logic.action: Dispense only if the pharmacy is certified and the prescriber's completed Prescriber Agreement Form came with the prescription or is on file; then dispense for delivery within 4 calendar days of receiving the prescription, or confirm appropriateness with the prescriber and document the decision, and record the NDC and lot number.

decision_logic.condition: A pharmacy is asked to lend, sell or transfer mifepristone.
decision_logic.action: Distribute, transfer, loan or sell it only to certified prescribers or other locations of the same pharmacy.

Do not require REMS enrollment or REMS verification of eligibility or ANC; provide the Medication Guide under 21 CFR 208.24(e); and treat FDA's ANC-monitoring recommendation as addressed to prescribers rather than as a dispensing condition.

ma_vs_federal.text: The Medication Guide and REMS requirements in this section are federal. They apply to a pharmacist and pharmacy in Massachusetts alongside Massachusetts law, and where both reach the same dispensing the pharmacist satisfies both, so the stricter requirement governs.

Part 208 regulates the provision of a document and says nothing about counseling. 21 CFR 208.24(e) yields only to an exemption under 21 CFR 208.26, and a patient's declining to discuss the medication is not one, so the Guide is provided whatever happens to a Massachusetts offer to counsel, which is taught in its own section.
Mifepristone REMS requirements apply to a certified pharmacy in Massachusetts in addition to the ordinary requirements of Massachusetts law for prescription drugs; neither layer removes the other.
FDA's removal of the Clozapine REMS ended a federal program requirement; it says nothing about any Massachusetts requirement, such as prospective drug review, which is taught in its own section.

exceptions.text: Part 208 applies primarily, not only, to products used on an outpatient basis without direct supervision by a health professional.
A prescriber's patient-specific direction under 21 CFR 208.26(b) is an exemption from the dispensing duty, but it yields whenever the patient requests information when the product is dispensed.
FDA may exempt or defer Medication Guide content or format requirements under 21 CFR 208.26(a), except the requirements in 21 CFR 208.20(a)(2) and (a)(6).

FDA's guidance describes enforcement discretion, not a regulatory exemption, for drugs dispensed to healthcare professionals for administration, and that discretion does not extend to a request by the patient or the patient's agent or to REMS terms that require the Guide.

A certified pharmacy may dispense mifepristone for delivery more than 4 calendar days after receiving the prescription once it has confirmed appropriateness with the prescriber and documented the prescriber's decision.
A certified pharmacy may distribute, transfer, loan or sell mifepristone to certified prescribers and to other locations of the pharmacy.

timing_deadlines.event: Dispensing of a product for which a Medication Guide is required
timing_deadlines.timeframe: When the product is dispensed, on new prescriptions and refills
timing_deadlines.consequence: The authorized dispenser provides the Guide directly to the patient or the patient's agent unless an exemption under 21 CFR 208.26 applies.

timing_deadlines.event: A patient's request for information where the prescriber has directed that the Guide not be provided
timing_deadlines.timeframe: When the drug product is dispensed
timing_deadlines.consequence: The authorized dispenser provides the Guide regardless of the prescriber's direction.

timing_deadlines.timeframe: Before the Guide may be distributed
timing_deadlines.consequence: The manufacturer obtains FDA approval of the Guide.

timing_deadlines.event: A drug dispensed to a healthcare professional for administration in an outpatient setting
timing_deadlines.timeframe: The first time it is dispensed there, and the first time a drug is dispensed in any outpatient setting after the Guide is materially changed
timing_deadlines.consequence: FDA's guidance expects the Guide to be provided; for later dispensings FDA intends to exercise enforcement discretion unless the patient or agent requests the Guide or a REMS requires it.

timing_deadlines.event: A certified pharmacy receives a mifepristone prescription
timing_deadlines.timeframe: Delivery to the patient within 4 calendar days of the date the pharmacy receives the prescription
timing_deadlines.consequence: For delivery after that period the pharmacy confirms appropriateness with the prescriber and documents the prescriber's decision, and the prescriber assesses appropriateness when contacted.

timing_deadlines.event: A certified pharmacy places its first order of mifepristone
timing_deadlines.timeframe: Sponsor audit within 180 calendar days, then annually for certified pharmacies that ordered in the previous 12 months
timing_deadlines.consequence: The pharmacy complies with audits carried out by the Mifepristone Sponsors or a third party acting for them, and Sponsors de-certify pharmacies that do not maintain compliance.

timing_deadlines.event: Verification of a certified pharmacy's authorized representative
timing_deadlines.consequence: If the name and contact information differ from the current designated representative, the Sponsor requires the pharmacy to recertify with the new authorized representative.

timing_deadlines.event: Modification of the Mifepristone REMS Program
timing_deadlines.consequence: The in-person dispensing requirement was removed and pharmacy certification added; retail pharmacies that meet the program requirements are eligible for certification.
Prescribers, pharmacies and patients are no longer required to participate in the REMS program or report ANC results to it for clozapine to be dispensed.

forms_records.text: The container label, or the package label where the container label is too small, carries the instruction to the authorized dispenser to provide a Medication Guide and states how the Guide is provided.

The Medication Guide itself is FDA-approved patient labeling; the words Medication Guide appear prominently at the top of its first page and FDA's verbatim approval statement appears at its bottom, requirements FDA cannot exempt.
A manufacturer supplies either Guides or the means to produce them, and a distributor or packer passes whichever it receives to each authorized dispenser to whom it ships a container of the product.

Prescriber Agreement Form: completed by a healthcare provider to become certified to prescribe mifepristone, provided by the certified prescriber to a certified pharmacy that will dispense or to an authorized distributor where the prescriber dispenses or supervises dispensing, received by the pharmacy with the prescription or kept on file, and retained in the pharmacy's records.
Pharmacy Agreement Form: completed by the pharmacy's authorized representative, committing the pharmacy to the program's processes and procedures.

Patient Agreement Form: reviewed with the patient, signed by the patient and the healthcare provider, copied to the patient together with the Medication Guide, and placed in the patient's medical record; in this REMS a signature includes an electronic signature.

The patient's record at a certified pharmacy holds the NDC and lot number from each package of mifepristone dispensed, and the pharmacy documents the prescriber's decision where the patient will receive mifepristone more than 4 calendar days after the pharmacy received the prescription.
A certified pharmacy keeps records of Prescriber Agreement Forms, of dispensing and shipping, and of all its processes and procedures including compliance with them.
A certified prescriber who dispenses mifepristone or supervises its dispensing ensures that the NDC and lot number from each package dispensed are recorded in the patient's record.
For clozapine no REMS enrollment or REMS ANC report is part of ordering or dispensing since the removal; the patient document is the Medication Guide in the prescribing information.

role_duties.role: Authorized dispenser, such as the dispensing pharmacist
role_duties.duty: Provide the Medication Guide directly to each patient or patient's agent when a product requiring one is dispensed, on new prescriptions and refills, unless an exemption under 21 CFR 208.26 applies, and provide it to any patient who requests information regardless of a prescriber's direction.

May direct that a particular patient not receive the Guide on determining that it is not in that patient's best interest because of significant concerns about its effect; the direction yields to the patient's request for information.
Obtain FDA approval of the Guide before distribution, and ensure Guides or the means to produce them are available in sufficient numbers to permit a Guide for each patient receiving a prescription.
Provide the Guides, or the means to produce them, received from the manufacturer to each authorized dispenser to whom it ships a container of the product.

Determine in writing when patient labeling is necessary; exempt or defer Guide content or format requirements on its own initiative or an applicant's written request, except 21 CFR 208.20(a)(2) and (a)(6); determine whether a REMS is necessary and which elements it includes.

role_duties.role: Applicant or responsible person under a REMS
role_duties.duty: Submit a proposed REMS when FDA so determines and informs it; develop any Medication Guide or patient package insert and conduct any communication plan the REMS requires.

May be required by the REMS for a particular drug to be specially certified, to dispense only in certain health care settings, or to dispense only with evidence or other documentation of safe-use conditions, and may have its implementation of those elements monitored and evaluated through the applicant's implementation system.

role_duties.role: Certified pharmacy under the Mifepristone REMS
role_duties.duty: Keep email and fax receipt and tracked shipping; act through an authorized representative; verify prescriber certification; dispense for delivery within 4 calendar days or confirm with the prescriber and document; record NDC and lot numbers; track shipments; dispense in the package as supplied; report deaths to the prescriber and notify the Sponsor; restrict transfers; keep records; protect confidentiality; train staff; and comply with Sponsor audits.

role_duties.role: Pharmacy's authorized representative under the Mifepristone REMS
role_duties.duty: Carry out the certification process for the pharmacy, review the Prescribing Information, complete the Pharmacy Agreement Form and oversee implementation and compliance.

role_duties.role: Certified prescriber under the Mifepristone REMS
role_duties.duty: Hold the attested abilities; review the Patient Agreement Form with the patient and explain the risks, sign it with the patient, give the patient a copy and the Medication Guide, and place it in the medical record; report deaths to the Sponsor; provide a signed Prescriber Agreement Form to a certified pharmacy that will dispense, and assess appropriateness when that pharmacy calls about delivery after 4 calendar days.
Sign a Patient Agreement Form indicating receipt of a copy and counseling from the healthcare provider on the risk of serious complications.

Certify and de-certify prescribers and pharmacies, verify authorized representatives annually, audit certified pharmacies, and ship only to certified pharmacies or locations identified by certified prescribers.

role_duties.role: Clozapine prescriber after the REMS removal
role_duties.duty: No REMS enrollment or ANC reporting to a REMS; FDA recommends monitoring ANC before starting clozapine and during treatment according to the prescribing information and counseling patients about the risk of severe neutropenia.

role_duties.role: Pharmacy and pharmacist dispensing clozapine after the REMS removal
role_duties.duty: Order from wholesaler distributors without REMS enrollment and dispense without REMS verification of patient eligibility, including ANC monitoring, while providing the Medication Guide under 21 CFR 208.24(e).

common_traps.text: Treating the Guide as a first-fill document. Part 208 applies to new prescriptions and refill prescriptions.
Withholding the Guide because a family member or neighbour is collecting. The Guide goes to the patient or the patient's agent when the product is dispensed.
Treating a prescriber's direction as final. A patient who requests information when the product is dispensed receives the Guide regardless, and the request need not be written or name the Guide.
Reading 21 CFR 208.26(a) as an exemption a pharmacist may invoke. It is FDA's power over content and format, exercised on its own initiative or an applicant's written request.

Carrying FDA's inpatient enforcement discretion to the retail counter, or treating it as part of the regulation. It is nonbinding guidance, and dispensing directly to a patient or caregiver is outside it.
Treating a Medication Guide and a REMS as the same thing. A REMS may require a Guide, but FDA may approve a Guide under Part 208 without requiring a REMS, as clozapine's labeling now shows.
Stating a pharmacy duty as common to every REMS. Pharmacy certification and dispensing conditions are elements a particular REMS may require.
Recalling the pre-2023 Mifepristone REMS. In-person dispensing is no longer required, pharmacy certification is, and retail pharmacies are eligible for certification.

Treating certification as a pharmacy's only mifepristone obligation. The pharmacy also verifies the prescriber, observes the 4-calendar-day delivery standard, records NDC and lot numbers and restricts transfers.
Putting the Patient Agreement Form on the pharmacy. The certified prescriber ensures it is reviewed, signed, copied to the patient and filed.

Continuing to enforce the Clozapine REMS gate, or concluding that its removal ended the Medication Guide. Enrollment and REMS verification are gone; the Boxed Warning and a new Medication Guide remain.

drug_examples.teaching_point: Mifepristone 200 mg for medical termination of pregnancy through ten weeks gestation is dispensed under the Mifepristone REMS Program: by or under the supervision of a certified prescriber, or by a certified pharmacy on a certified prescriber's prescription, which dispenses for delivery within 4 calendar days of receiving the prescription or confirms appropriateness with the prescriber and documents the decision.

Clozapine has had no REMS since June 13, 2025, so pharmacies need no enrollment to order and no eligibility or ANC verification before dispensing, but its labeling carries a Boxed Warning and a new Medication Guide that the authorized dispenser provides under 21 CFR 208.24(e).
